pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — Animal Migration (ages 7–9): regular, seasonal, long-distance journeys many animals make and back again, driven by the need for food, breeding sites, or to escape harsh seasons.
• Standards — UK (DfE): extends KS1/KS2 habitats-and-adaptation; introduces migration as a BEHAVIOURAL response to seasonal habitat change (links to 'environments can change').
• Standards — US (NGSS): 3-LS4-3 (survival in a changing habitat); 3-LS1-1 relevance (life cycles include breeding journeys); reinforces that habitats change over time.
• Operational details: define migration as a REGULAR, seasonal, round-trip movement (distinguish from a one-off wandering). Anchor ≥3 migrants with their routes — Arctic tern (pole-to-pole), monarch butterfly (multi-generation to Mexico), wildebeest (Serengeti loop), humpback whale (feeding↔breeding), swallow (UK↔Africa), salmon (sea↔river to spawn). Establish the drivers: following food, reaching breeding grounds, escaping winter/dry season. Touch on how animals navigate (sun, stars, magnetic field, landmarks) at an age-appropriate level.
• Checkpoint — A (concrete, ~7–8): name an animal that migrates and say where it goes and why. B (transitional, ~8–9): explain that migration is a there-AND-back seasonal journey driven by food/breeding/season, with an example route. C (formal, ~9): distinguish migration from other movement and name at least one navigation cue animals use.
bestPractices: Nail the definition with the round-trip criterion — there AND back, on a seasonal schedule — so pupils don't count any long movement as migration.
Map real routes on a world map so the journey's scale and destinations are concrete (an Arctic tern's pole-to-pole path is a powerful hook).
Sort each example by its DRIVER (food, breeding, escaping a harsh season) so pupils see migration as problem-solving, not instinctive wandering.
Introduce navigation with tangible cues (sun position, Earth's magnetism, landmarks, smell for salmon) so 'how do they find the way?' has real answers, avoiding the 'they just know' dead end.
keyRepresentations: A world map with animated migration routes (arrows out and back) for several species.
A seasonal calendar wheel linking each leg of a journey to a season and its reason (breed / feed / escape cold).
A compass/magnet-and-sun diagram illustrating navigation cues.
A before/after habitat pair (summer feeding ground vs winter breeding ground) for one migrant.
commonMisconceptions: 'Any long journey is migration' — migration is regular, seasonal, and a round trip, not a one-off move.
'Only birds migrate' — mammals (whales, wildebeest), fish (salmon), insects (monarchs) and others migrate too.
'Animals migrate because they get bored/cold and just leave' — the drivers are specific: food, breeding, or escaping a harsh season.
'The same individual butterfly flies all the way to Mexico and back' — the monarch round trip spans multiple generations.
'Animals have no way to navigate — they just know' — they use real cues: sun, stars, Earth's magnetic field, landmarks, smell.

learn.summary: Help 7–9 year-olds understand animal migration as a regular round-trip journey (usually seasonal and yearly; for salmon a once-in-a-lifetime round trip, for monarchs one spread over several generations) driven by food, breeding, or escaping a harsh season — not any one-off long movement. Learners map real routes for several species (Arctic tern, monarch, wildebeest, humpback whale, swallow, salmon), link each leg of a journey to a season and its reason, and explore how animals navigate using real cues (sun, stars, Earth's magnetic field, landmarks, smell). The centrepiece is a season-driven map the learner runs, so migration appears as a timed response to a changing habitat; map-reveal, sorting, and recall activities support and check the same ideas.

activities.title: Run a season-driven migration map
feedback: If a learner leaves the animal in one place and the meter drops: 'The food/breeding ground has moved with the season — where does the animal need to be now to survive?'
When a learner completes the out-and-back cycle: 'Notice it's a round trip on a schedule — out when conditions change, back when the other place becomes best again.'

On the monarch route: 'The monarchs that fly south to Mexico in autumn make that whole leg themselves, but the butterfly that leaves Mexico in spring is not the one that arrives back in the north — the round trip is a relay across several generations.'
activities.rationale: Turning the dial and watching the habitat move is intended to make the seasonal driver and the round-trip criterion something the learner enacts rather than reads, addressing 'any long journey is migration' and 'animals just wander/get bored'. A calendar wheel linking each leg to a season and reason, and a generation counter for the monarch, make the mechanism concrete. The direction of the 'good' habitat is species-dependent and the interaction details are optional examples, not required mechanisms; the approach is a proposal that has not been tested here.
sourceClaims: Migration is a regular, seasonal, round-trip movement driven by food, breeding, or escaping a harsh season; migrants include Arctic tern (pole-to-pole), monarch (multi-generation), wildebeest, humpback whale, swallow, salmon.
Migration is a behavioural response to seasonal habitat change; extends KS1/KS2 habitats-and-adaptation and 'environments can change'.
learnerActions: Pick a migrant (e.g. swallow, Arctic tern, wildebeest) and watch where it starts on a world map.

Turn a calendar/season dial and observe the 'good' habitat move across the map — for example grass greening in a summer feeding region, or breeding waters warming in a breeding region — while the animal's food/breeding meter responds. (Which direction is 'good' depends on the species: swallows breed in the northern summer, humpback whales breed in warm tropical waters.)
Move the animal to follow the shifting habitat, discovering that staying put makes the food or breeding meter drop.
Advance through a full year so the animal travels out AND back, matching each leg to a season and its reason (feed / breed / escape harsh season).
For the monarch route, watch a generation counter show that the animal that sets out is often not the one that arrives.
activities.intendedInsight: Migration is a regular, seasonal, there-and-back journey that an animal makes because the habitat offering food or breeding sites shifts with the seasons — it is purposeful, not aimless wandering, and for monarchs the round trip spans multiple generations.

activities.title: Steer by the animal's navigation cues
feedback: When the right cue keeps the route: 'That cue helped keep the animal on track — this is one real way animals find their way.'

When a cue is mismatched and the route wanders: 'Cues help the animal stay on course — real migrants usually combine several of these cues, so navigation is a real skill, not something they magically know.'
On salmon: 'Salmon can smell their way back to the river where they hatched.'
activities.rationale: Giving the learner the animal's cues is intended to make 'how do they find the way?' have concrete answers and replace the 'they just know' dead end. The one-cue-at-a-time control is a game simplification; real animals integrate multiple cues, so feedback avoids implying an animal relies on a single cue. Interaction details are illustrative options, not mandatory, and efficacy is untested here.
sourceClaims: Migrating animals navigate using cues including the sun, stars, Earth's magnetic field, landmarks and (for salmon) smell.
learnerActions: Take control of a migrant and try to stay on its route, using the animal's real cues: the sun's position, the stars, Earth's magnetic field, coastal landmarks, or (for salmon) the smell of its home river.
Try the cues one at a time as a game, then notice that real animals often use several cues together to stay on course.
Match each cue to an animal that famously uses it (e.g. salmon and home-river smell).
activities.intendedInsight: Animals do not 'just know' the way — they use real, nameable cues (sun, stars, Earth's magnetic field, landmarks, smell), often several together, to navigate long journeys.

activities.title: Map and label real migration routes
feedback: If a learner thinks only birds migrate: 'Whales, wildebeest, salmon and monarch butterflies migrate too — migration is not just a bird thing.'
When a route is traced: 'This animal travels this far for a reason — is it chasing food, reaching a breeding ground, or escaping a harsh season?'
activities.rationale: Mapping real routes makes the journeys' scale and destinations concrete (the Arctic tern's pole-to-pole path is a strong hook) and spreads examples across animal groups to counter 'only birds migrate'. A static or tappable map reveals where and why but does not by itself let the learner link seasons to legs dynamically — pair it with the season-driven map for that.
sourceClaims: Migration is a regular, seasonal, round-trip movement driven by food, breeding, or escaping a harsh season; migrants include Arctic tern (pole-to-pole), monarch (multi-generation), wildebeest, humpback whale, swallow, salmon.
learnerActions: On a world map, tap or trace the route of at least three migrants out and back.
For each, read or reveal why it goes (following food, reaching breeding grounds, escaping winter/dry season) and roughly how far.

Pair a summer feeding ground with a winter breeding ground for a migrant that fits this pattern (e.g. humpback whale: polar summer feeding, tropical winter breeding) to see the before/after habitat contrast — swallows do the reverse, breeding in the northern summer.
activities.intendedInsight: Real migrants span many animal groups — birds (Arctic tern, swallow), mammals (whale, wildebeest), fish (salmon), insects (monarch) — and each route has a destination and a reason, making the scale and purpose of the journeys concrete.

activities.title: The return-trip puzzle (talk and reason)
feedback: If a learner says they should just stay where it's warm: 'If it were only about warmth, they'd never come back. In the northern spring and summer there's a burst of insects to eat and safe places to nest — that's why they return.'
If a learner confuses migration with hibernation: 'Hibernators stay put and sleep through winter; migrators travel. Which is the swallow doing?'
If a learner describes it as a planned holiday: 'Animals don't book a trip — the journey is an inherited instinct triggered by cues such as the days getting shorter.'
activities.rationale: The return-trip puzzle discriminates the naive 'escape the cold' idea (which predicts the bird should just stay warm) from a food-and-breeding seasonal account (which explains the return). Sorting migration vs hibernation and discussing the what-if targets the specific recorded misconceptions. Spoken reasoning and responsive discussion let a teacher probe the return leg directly; a sort can check whether a learner classifies migrate vs hibernate but does not by itself elicit the explanation.
sourceClaims: Migration is a regular, seasonal, round-trip movement driven by food, breeding, or escaping a harsh season; migrants include Arctic tern (pole-to-pole), monarch (multi-generation), wildebeest, humpback whale, swallow, salmon.
Migration is a behavioural response to seasonal habitat change; extends KS1/KS2 habitats-and-adaptation and 'environments can change'.
learnerActions: Consider: every autumn swallows fly thousands of miles from Britain to Africa, then fly all the way back in spring — why not just stay in warm Africa all year? Why make the journey twice?
State a reason the swallows come BACK, not just why they leave.
Decide and explain: is a hedgehog that sleeps all winter migrating? Sort several animals into 'migrates' vs 'hibernates'.
Name another animal that migrates and say what it is travelling towards.

Answer a what-if: if there were plenty of insects in Britain all winter, would the swallows still leave? (Discuss both sides: the urge to leave is inherited and triggered by cues like shortening days, so many might still go, but over many generations food availability shapes where and whether a species migrates.)
activities.intendedInsight: Migration follows food and breeding across the seasons, not just warmth — which is why there is a return leg. It is distinct from hibernation (stay put and sleep) and is an inherited, instinctive pattern triggered by cues like shortening daylight, not a human-like planned choice.

activities.title: Check the definition: match, sequence, define
feedback: For 'same butterfly does the whole round trip': 'The monarch round trip spans several generations — no single butterfly makes the whole round trip, even though one generation does fly all the way south to Mexico.'

For a one-off move chosen as migration: 'Migration is a regular there-and-back pattern, usually repeated every year with the seasons (salmon make it once in a lifetime, monarchs across generations) — a single move away is not migration.'
activities.rationale: Matching, sequencing and multiple-choice can check the round-trip definition and surface 'only birds migrate' and 'one butterfly does the whole trip'. These items check and consolidate the definition rather than building the seasonal intuition, so use them after the enactive and discussion activities.
sourceClaims: Migration is a regular, seasonal, round-trip movement driven by food, breeding, or escaping a harsh season; migrants include Arctic tern (pole-to-pole), monarch (multi-generation), wildebeest, humpback whale, swallow, salmon.
learnerActions: Match each migrant to its route and its driver (food / breeding / escaping a harsh season).
Put the legs of one journey in the correct order by season.
Choose the statement that correctly defines migration and separate it from a one-off wandering move.
Identify the error in statements like 'the same butterfly flies all the way to Mexico and back' or 'only birds migrate'.
activities.intendedInsight: Migration is defined by being regular, seasonal, and a round trip — and learners can apply that definition to tell true migration from one-off movement and to catch common mistakes.

constraints: Define migration with the round-trip criterion — there AND back, on a regular (usually seasonal, yearly) schedule — so a one-off long movement is not counted as migration; note that for some species the round trip spans a lifetime (salmon return from the sea to their home river years later) or several generations (monarchs).
Include migrants from several animal groups (birds, mammals, fish, insects), not only birds.
Sort each example by its driver (food, breeding, escaping a harsh season) so migration reads as purposeful problem-solving, not aimless/random wandering; distinguish it clearly from hibernation.
Present the monarch as a multi-generation relay: the individual setting out is often not the one that arrives.

Describe navigation with concrete cues (sun, stars, Earth's magnetic field, landmarks, smell), note that real animals often combine several cues, and avoid the 'they just know' explanation; also avoid implying a conscious human-like plan — frame it as inherited instinct triggered by cues like shortening daylight.
Matching/sequence/multiple-choice items check and consolidate the definition but do not by themselves build the seasonal-driver intuition; use them after enactive and discussion work.
A tappable or static route map reveals where and why but does not let learners link seasons to legs dynamically; pair it with a season-driven map or discussion for that.

The direction of the 'good' habitat (feeding vs breeding ground) is species-dependent — swallows breed in the northern summer, humpback whales breed in warm tropical waters — so do not present 'breeding is always south/warm' as a rule.

Interaction examples (season dial, moving habitat, cue-steering, generation counter, lift-the-flap cards) are illustrative options, not required mechanisms, and a 3D globe is optional dramatisation not needed for the core idea.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; all listed sources remain marked verified:false and were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Source claims about migration drivers, species routes, and navigation cues come from general natural-history/behavioural-ecology references and standards documents (DfE KS1/KS2, NGSS 3-LS4-3/3-LS1-1) that were not independently re-checked here.

The 'escape winter/dry season' driver and the food/breeding account are age-appropriate simplifications; actual migration triggers vary by species and the climate details (e.g. 'plenty of insects in Britain all winter') are hypotheticals for reasoning, not claims about real conditions.
The cue-steering activity uses one cue at a time as a game mechanic; real migrants typically integrate multiple cues, so feedback was softened to avoid implying reliance on a single cue.

Whether the 'good' habitat lies to the warm south or the summer north depends on the species and on whether the leg is for feeding or breeding; the dial example is illustrative and should not be generalised into a fixed direction.

The source material uses 'instinctive wandering' (not migration) in one place and 'inherited instinct' (for migration) in another; the guidance resolves this by describing migration as purposeful/not aimless AND as inherited instinct not a conscious plan, which are consistent once the two senses are separated.

probeDeeper: Why do the swallows come BACK in spring instead of staying in Africa?
Name another animal that migrates, and say what it is travelling towards.
Is a hedgehog that sleeps all winter migrating? Why or why not?
What if there were plenty of insects in Britain all winter — would the swallows still leave?
assess.correctAnswer: They return because migration follows food and breeding, not just warmth. In the northern spring and summer there are huge numbers of insects to eat, long daylight, and good, safe places to nest and raise young; by autumn that food runs out, so they travel back to Africa where food is plentiful over winter. Each place gives them what they need at that time of year, so the round trip is worth it — it's about food and raising young, not simply escaping the cold.

errorPatterns.pattern: Animals migrate just to escape the cold and get to warm weather
errorPatterns.nextMove: Shift the driver from temperature to food and breeding; point to the summer burst of insects and safe nesting as the reason to come back.
errorPatterns.distractor: Because Africa is warm and Britain is cold — so they should just stay in Africa.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says they should stay where it is warm; is puzzled about why they ever return.

errorPatterns.pattern: Migration is the same as hibernation — the animals sleep through winter
errorPatterns.nextMove: Contrast the two strategies — hibernators stay put and sleep, migrators travel; sort examples into the two groups.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Describes migrating animals as sleeping or resting rather than travelling.

errorPatterns.pattern: The animals plan and choose the trip, like people booking a holiday
errorPatterns.nextMove: Explain migration as an inherited, instinctive seasonal pattern triggered by cues such as shortening daylight, not a conscious plan.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Describes a deliberate, human-like decision to travel.

responseLevels.gap: Describes migration only as escaping the cold or going somewhere warm, or confuses it with hibernation; can't explain the return journey.
responseLevels.full: Explains migration as driven by food, breeding and the seasons — travelling to where food and safe nesting are available at each time of year — names several migrators with destinations, explains the return leg, and distinguishes migration from hibernation.
responseLevels.partial: Defines migration as a long, regular journey and names an example, but gives only one driver (usually warmth) and can't fully explain the round trip or link it to food and breeding across the seasons.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Every autumn, swallows fly thousands of miles from Britain all the way to Africa — and then fly the whole way back again in spring. Why don't they just stay in warm Africa all year? Why make the journey twice?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The naive 'escape the cold' idea predicts the bird should just stay where it's warm — it cannot explain the return leg. Only a food-and-breeding, seasonal account explains why the swallows come back. The return-trip puzzle is what separates the two reasoning paths.
